skills.name: Memory Mountain
skills.learn: Hold a few things in your mind at once.
skills.tip: Say it quietly to yourself, or make a picture in your head.

card.title: Your brain has a notepad
card.text: Working memory holds things for a short time. Saying them again helps them stay.

spec: Elephant grandmothers remember where to find water, even after many years.
skills.why: Many kids with ADHD have a smaller mental notepad; repeating, picturing and chunking are tools that give it more room.

skills.name: Plan Builder
skills.learn: Put steps in order and break big jobs into small ones.
skills.tip: Ask: what is the very first step?

card.title: Big jobs, small steps
card.text: A big job is just many small steps. Do one step, then the next.

spec: Beavers build a dam one stick and one scoop of mud at a time.
skills.why: Kids with ADHD often see a big task as one overwhelming block; practicing "first step" thinking and checklists makes starting easier.

skills.name: Time Tracker
skills.learn: Notice what comes before and after, and how long things take.
skills.tip: A timer lets you see time move.

card.title: Seeing time
card.text: Time is hard to feel. Timers and picture schedules help you see it.

spec: Morning glory flowers open in the morning and close later in the day.
skills.why: ADHD can make time feel invisible ("time blindness"); timers, schedules and estimate-then-check practice make it visible.

skills.name: Flex Forest
skills.learn: Find a Plan B and try more than one way.
skills.tip: Say: "That is OK. What is my Plan B?"

card.title: Bend, don't break
card.text: Plans can change. It is OK to feel upset. Then we find a Plan B.

spec: An octopus can change its color and shape to fit where it is.
skills.why: Changes can feel very hard for kids with ADHD or autism; naming the feeling and rehearsing Plan B thinking builds calm, confident flexibility.

skills.name: Check-It Castle
skills.learn: Look back at your work and fix what you find.
skills.tip: Read it once more before you say "done."

card.title: Be a work detective
card.text: Everyone makes mistakes. Checking helps you find and fix them.

spec: Scout honeybees check many new home spots before the swarm picks one.
skills.why: Quick, impulsive finishing is common with ADHD; a friendly checking routine catches slips and turns mistakes into something to find, not fear.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Say the names: cat, sun, star.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Say the names: apple, dog, moon.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Count them on your fingers as you say each name.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Picture a frog in a house, eating a banana, kicking a ball.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Make a picture: a bee flies over a rainbow to a rocket.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Make a silly story: a pizza holds a key, a turtle eats a strawberry on a train.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Group them: school things (pencil, books), animals (elephant, lion), and a present.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Chunk them into two groups of three: cat, apple, car. Then dog, moon, star.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Say all six names quietly, then say them once more.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Make a picture: a frog kicks a banana like a ball, all the way to a rocket.

items.prompt: Your teacher says, “Get your pencil, then your book.” What do you get first?

choices.why: The book comes second. The pencil comes first.
The teacher did not say backpack. Listen for pencil and book.

items.explain: The teacher said pencil first, then book. Saying the steps again helps you remember.
items.hint: Say the words again: pencil, then book.

items.prompt: You need to remember three things. What can help?

choices.why: A different song can push the words out. Saying them helps them stay.
Hoping is hard work for a brain. Saying them again works better.

items.explain: Saying things again quietly keeps them on your brain notepad.
items.hint: Which one uses the words you need to remember?

items.prompt: Mia needs to remember the number 5552914. Which trick helps most?

choices.why: One fast look is easy to lose. Chunks give your memory handles.

choices.t: Wait and try to remember it later
choices.why: Working memory fades fast. Chunking right away helps it stay.

items.explain: Chunking turns 7 numbers into 2 groups. Two groups are much easier to hold.
items.hint: Phone numbers are often said in groups. Which choice uses groups?

items.prompt: Mr. Lee says: put away math, get your reading book, then line up. Jay forgets the middle step. What could Jay do?

choices.t: Kindly ask Mr. Lee to say it again

choices.why: A guess might be the wrong step. Asking gets the real answer.

choices.t: Stay in his seat and worry
choices.why: Worrying does not bring the step back. Asking is a brave, helpful tool.

items.explain: Forgetting a step happens to everyone. Asking again, or writing steps down, are smart tools.
items.hint: Which choice gets Jay the real direction?

items.prompt: Ava must buy milk, eggs, and bread. Which idea makes a picture in her mind?

choices.t: Picture a cow juggling eggs and bread
Say the list out loud three times
choices.why: That is a great tool too! But it uses words, not a picture.

choices.t: Count the items on her fingers
choices.why: That helps too, but it uses fingers, not a picture.

items.explain: A silly mind picture is easy to remember. The cow stands for milk!
items.hint: Look for the choice you could see with your eyes closed.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to get your feet ready.
items.explain: Socks go on before shoes. You fasten shoes after they are on.
items.hint: What goes on your feet first?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to brush your teeth.
items.explain: Toothpaste goes on first. You rinse after you brush.
items.hint: What do you need on the brush before you start?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to plant a seed.
items.explain: You need a hole before the seed. The seed sprouts last, after it is planted.
items.hint: What do you need before you can drop in a seed?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to make a jam sandwich.
items.explain: You need bread first. The jam goes on before you close the sandwich.
items.hint: What do you need before you can spread jam?

items.prompt: Your room is messy. It feels too big! What do you do first?

choices.why: Big jobs can feel hard. Small steps make it easier.
All at once is too much. One small step works better.

items.explain: One small job at a time makes a big job easier. Toys first, then the next thing!
items.hint: Which choice is one small step?

items.prompt: It is library day. What goes in your bag?

choices.why: A pan stays in the kitchen. Library day needs your book.
A couch is way too big for a bag! Library day needs your book.

items.explain: On library day, you bring back your library book.
items.hint: What do you need at the library?

items.prompt: Your list says: folder, lunch, water bottle. You packed the folder and lunch. What is left?

choices.why: The folder has a check. It is packed.
Lunch has a check. It is packed.

items.explain: The empty box shows what is left. A checklist remembers for you!
items.hint: Look for the box with no check.

items.prompt: Put the steps of a science project in order.
steps: 💭 Make a guess about the answer
items.explain: You need a question before a guess, and a test before results. Sharing comes last.
items.hint: Every project starts with something you wonder about.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to mail a letter.
steps: 📮 Seal the envelope and add a stamp
items.explain: The letter must be written before it goes in the envelope. It is mailed only when sealed and stamped.
items.hint: What has to exist before anything goes in the envelope?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to write a book report.
items.explain: You need to read before you write. You check your draft before you turn it in.
items.hint: What must you do before you can write about a book?

items.prompt: Maya has a big project due Friday. It is Monday. What is the best plan?

choices.t: Split it into a small part for each day

choices.why: One late night can feel very stressful. Small daily parts feel easier.

choices.t: Wait until she feels like starting
choices.why: That feeling may not come. A plan helps you start anyway.

items.explain: Breaking a big job into small daily parts makes each day doable.
items.hint: Which plan uses more than one day?

items.prompt: Homework feels huge tonight. What is a good first step?

choices.t: List the tasks and pick where to start
Stare at the pile and worry
choices.why: Worry makes the pile feel bigger. A list makes it smaller.

choices.t: Put it all off until bedtime
choices.why: Tired brains find homework harder. Earlier is usually easier.

items.explain: A list turns one big scary pile into small tasks you can check off.
items.hint: Which choice breaks the big job into parts?

items.prompt: Leo often forgets his gym shoes on Tuesdays. Which tool could help?

choices.t: Pack them Monday night using a checklist

choices.why: Trying harder rarely works alone. Brains love reminders they can see.
Gym is fun and good for your body. A tool can solve this.

items.explain: Packing the night before, with a checklist, means the morning brain has less to remember.
items.hint: Which choice uses a tool you can see?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to wash your hands.
items.explain: Soap goes on wet hands. You rinse the soap off, then dry last.
items.hint: What do you do before the soap?

items.prompt: Put the days in order.
items.explain: Yesterday was before today. Tomorrow comes after today.
items.hint: Which day already happened?

items.prompt: Put the parts of the day in order.
items.explain: The day starts in the morning. Afternoon is next. Night comes last.
items.hint: When do you wake up?

items.prompt: Which takes longer?

choices.why: Brushing takes about 2 minutes. A movie takes much longer.

items.explain: A movie takes about 1 or 2 hours. Brushing takes about 2 minutes.
items.hint: Which one can you finish in a song or two?

items.prompt: About how long does washing your hands take?

choices.why: An hour is as long as a whole TV show or more. Handwashing is quick.
A day is from morning to night. Handwashing is much faster.

items.explain: Washing and drying your hands takes about 1 minute.
items.hint: Is it quick or slow?

items.prompt: First you eat lunch. Then you go to recess. What comes right before recess?

choices.why: Bedtime is at night, long after recess.
You go home after school ends.

items.explain: Lunch comes first. Recess comes after lunch.
items.hint: Listen for the word first.

items.prompt: Your schedule shows reading, then art, then snack. What comes after art?

choices.why: Reading came before art.
Nap is not on the schedule.

items.explain: The arrows show what comes next. Snack comes after art.
items.hint: Find art. Follow the arrow.

items.prompt: The timer rings. Tablet time is done. You feel sad. What helps?

choices.why: Hiding it can break trust. Sad is OK. Pick a next fun thing.
Throwing can break it. Take a slow breath instead.

items.explain: It is OK to feel sad when fun time ends. Remembering “later” helps.
items.hint: Which choice is kind to you and the tablet?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to bake cookies.
items.explain: Dough is mixed before scooping and baked before cooling. Hot cookies must cool before eating.
items.hint: What has to exist before you can scoop?

items.prompt: Put the life of a butterfly in order.
items.explain: A butterfly starts as an egg. The caterpillar makes a chrysalis, then changes into a butterfly.
items.hint: Every butterfly starts very tiny.

items.prompt: Put these months in order, starting at the beginning of the year.
items.explain: The year starts with January. February, March, and April come next.
items.hint: Which month is New Year's Day in?

items.prompt: About how long does it take to read a picture book out loud?

choices.why: Ten seconds is barely enough for one page.
Ten hours is longer than a whole school day.

items.explain: Most picture books take about 5 to 10 minutes to read aloud.
items.hint: Count slowly to 10. Could you read a whole book that fast?

items.prompt: Zoe has 30 minutes before dinner. Her homework takes about 20 minutes. What is the best plan?

choices.why: Then all 30 minutes are used up before homework even starts.
Without checking, time can slip away. The clock helps her plan.

items.explain: 20 minutes of homework fits in 30 minutes, with 10 minutes left to relax.
items.hint: Which plan fits 20 minutes of work into 30 minutes?

items.prompt: Time runs out on a quiz, and Ali is not done. What is a kind, helpful plan?

choices.t: Take a breath and talk with the teacher
Decide he is just bad at quizzes
choices.why: One quiz does not decide who you are. Time tools can help.
That throws away the work he did. His effort still counts.

items.explain: Running out of time happens. A teacher can help make a plan, like more time or smaller parts.
items.hint: Which choice gets Ali some help?

items.prompt: Kai guessed a chore would take 5 minutes. It took 20. What helps his next guess?

choices.why: Guessing is a skill that grows with practice. Keep trying!
Using what really happened makes the next guess closer.

items.explain: Guess, time it, then use what you learned. That is how time sense grows.
items.hint: What did Kai learn from the real time?

items.prompt: The park is closed today. You feel sad. What is a good Plan B?

choices.why: It is OK to feel sad. A Plan B can help the day feel better.
Kicking can hurt your foot. Feeling upset is OK. Try a Plan B.

items.explain: It is OK to feel disappointed. A Plan B still gives you something fun.
items.hint: Which choice is a new fun plan?

items.prompt: 5 + 5 makes 10. Which is another way to make 10?

choices.why: 3 + 3 makes 6.
9 + 2 makes 11.

items.explain: 6 + 4 also makes 10. There is more than one way!
items.hint: Start at 6 and count up 4 more.

items.prompt: Your friend wants to play tag. You want blocks. What can you say?

choices.why: Your friend may feel left out. Taking turns is fair.
Your friend may feel confused. Try sharing ideas.

items.explain: Taking turns lets both friends play what they like.
items.hint: Which choice lets both of you have a turn?

items.prompt: There is a new rule in the game. Hop, do not run. What do you do?

choices.why: The rule changed. Games are fair when all use the new rule.
New rules can feel strange. Give it a try first!

items.explain: New rules can feel funny at first. Trying them is flexible thinking.
items.hint: What does the new rule say?

items.prompt: Your teacher is away. A new teacher is here. You feel worried. What helps?

choices.t: Take a breath and say hi

choices.why: Hiding can make the worry grow. A breath helps you feel safe.
The new teacher wants to help. Give them a chance.

items.explain: Changes can feel scary, and that is OK. A breath and a hello help.
items.hint: Which choice helps your body feel calm?

items.prompt: Old rule: sort by color. New rule: sort by shape. Where does the red square go?

choices.why: That was the old rule. The new rule is shape.

items.explain: The rule switched to shape. A square goes with the squares, any color.
items.hint: What is the new rule?

items.prompt: The field trip is moved because of rain. Sam feels disappointed. Which thought is flexible?

choices.t: “I am sad, but we can still go later.”

choices.why: The trip is moved, not canceled. This thought makes the feeling bigger.
Big words like never and ever are rarely true. Look for what is still good.

items.explain: Flexible thoughts name the feeling and still find hope. Both can be true.
items.hint: Which thought names the feeling and finds something good?

items.prompt: One way to solve 25 + 9 is to count up. Which is another good way?

choices.why: That subtracts. The problem asks us to add 9.
That leaves out the 5 in 25.

items.explain: 25 + 10 = 35, and 35 − 1 = 34. Adding 10 is easy, so this is a smart shortcut.
items.hint: 9 is just 1 less than 10.

items.prompt: At a friend's house, they play a card game with different rules. What is a flexible choice?

choices.t: Insist your rules are the only right ones
choices.why: Different rules are not wrong, just different.
You might miss the fun. New rules are worth a try.

items.explain: Many games have more than one set of rules. Trying theirs is flexible and friendly.
items.hint: Which choice keeps the game going?

items.prompt: Nia wants to write about sharks, but the library has no shark books. What is a good Plan B?

choices.t: Ask the librarian for other sources

choices.why: One missing book does not end the project. There are other ways.

choices.t: Wait until shark books show up
choices.why: That could take too long. A Plan B keeps her moving.

items.explain: Librarians can find websites, magazines, or videos. There is more than one path.
items.hint: Who at the library knows where information is?

items.prompt: Your group picks Ben's idea, not yours. You feel frustrated. What is a flexible choice?

choices.t: Try Ben's idea and add to it

choices.why: The group still needs you. Your ideas can help Ben's idea grow.
Arguing can hurt feelings and waste time. Frustration is OK, though.

items.explain: Feeling frustrated is normal. Adding to a team idea is still a way to share your thinking.
items.hint: Which choice keeps you on the team?

items.prompt: You wrote an answer. What should you do next?

choices.why: A quick check catches small mistakes. Everyone makes them!
Your work matters. Check it instead.

items.explain: Reading it again helps you find and fix little mistakes.
items.hint: Which choice looks back at your work?

items.prompt: Sam wrote 3 + 2 = 6. Is he right?

choices.why: Count the dots. 3 and 2 more makes 5.
Count again. 3 and 2 more makes 5.

items.explain: 3 + 2 = 5. Counting the dots is a great way to check.
items.hint: Count all the dots.

items.prompt: Look at this sentence. What needs fixing?

choices.why: A sentence needs a period at the end. Keep it!
The words are fine. Look at the first letter.

items.explain: The word I is always a capital letter.
items.hint: Look at the very first letter.

items.prompt: You are stuck on a problem. What can you do?

choices.why: Stuck is a normal part of learning. Help gets you going.
Copying does not help your brain learn. Ask instead.

items.explain: Everyone gets stuck. Asking for help is a strong, smart move.
items.hint: Which choice gets a grown-up to help?

items.prompt: Look at your checklist. What is left to do?
items.visual:
✅ Write your name
✅ Write the date
⬜ Answer every question

choices.why: Your name has a check. It is done.
The date has a check. It is done.

items.explain: The empty box shows what is left. Checklists help you finish.
items.hint: Find the box with no check.

items.prompt: Sam wrote 25 + 10 = 45. What should he check?

choices.why: The ones are right. 5 + 0 is 5. The slip is in the tens.
That is a good habit, but it will not fix this math.

items.explain: 2 tens + 1 ten = 3 tens, so the answer is 35. Checking place value finds the slip.
items.hint: Look at the tens digit in each number.

items.prompt: Kim solved 42 − 17 = 25. Which math sentence checks it by putting it back?

choices.why: That adds the wrong numbers. Add your answer to the part taken away.
That subtracts again. Adding back is how we check subtraction.

items.explain: If 25 + 17 gets back to 42, the subtraction is right. It does!
items.hint: Subtraction and addition undo each other.

items.prompt: Maria checks for capitals, end marks, and spelling. What did she miss?

choices.t: A capital M at the start

choices.why: There is a period at the end. That part is done.
Every word is spelled correctly. Look at the first letter.

items.explain: Sentences start with a capital letter, so "my" should be "My."
items.hint: Go through the checklist one item at a time.

items.prompt: Jordan finished a math page super fast. What is a smart next step?

choices.t: Check each answer before turning it in

choices.why: Fast work is great, and a quick check can still catch slips.
That throws away good work. Just check and fix what you find.

items.explain: A quick-thinking brain is a strength. A check routine makes it even stronger.
items.hint: Which choice looks back at the work?

items.prompt: Ella found a mistake in her own work. Which thought is most helpful?

choices.t: “Finding mistakes means my brain is working.”

choices.why: Everyone makes mistakes. Catching yours is a skill!

choices.t: “I should hide it from my teacher.”
choices.why: Mistakes help teachers know how to help. Fixing them is brave.

items.explain: Catching your own mistake is exactly what good checkers do. Be proud!
items.hint: Which thought is kind to Ella?

items.prompt: Ben had 8 apples and ate 3. His answer says 50 apples. What should he ask himself?

choices.t: Can I make the number bigger?
choices.why: Eating apples makes the number smaller, not bigger.

choices.t: Should I just circle it and move on?
choices.why: A quick sense check could catch this slip first.

items.explain: He started with 8, so he cannot end with 50. The answer is 5. Asking "does it make sense?" catches big slips.
items.hint: Can you end with more apples after eating some?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to check a math answer.
steps: 🔁 Put your answer back to check
🛠️ Fix it if it does not match
items.explain: You need an answer before you can check it. You fix only after checking shows a problem.
items.hint: What do you need before you can check?

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Say the names: duck, cookie, bike.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Picture a bear on a bus, eating grapes, holding a sunflower.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Make a picture: a rabbit puts a carrot in a basket by a tulip.

items.prompt: Mom says, “Shoes, coat, hat.” What do you put on last?

choices.why: Shoes come first. Hat comes last.
Coat is in the middle. Hat comes last.

items.explain: Mom said shoes, then coat, then hat. The last word was hat. Saying it again helps you remember.
items.hint: Say it again: shoes, coat, hat.

items.prompt: You need to remember to feed the fish. What can help?

choices.t: Put a picture note by the fish tank
Keep it only in your head
choices.why: Heads get busy. A note you can see remembers for you.

choices.t: Wait for the fish to ask
choices.why: Fish cannot talk! A note helps you remember.

items.explain: A note or picture you can see is a helper for your memory.
items.hint: Which choice is something you can see?

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Make a silly story: a fox plays guitar, eats a donut, and flies a helicopter over a cactus.

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then find the one that is missing.
items.tip: Group them: animals (penguin, crab), foods (cheese, corn), and fun things (trumpet, balloon).

items.prompt: Watch the pictures. Then tap them in the same order.
items.tip: Chunk them into two groups of three: octopus, lemon, rocket. Then snail, dice, bell.

items.prompt: The directions are: do problems 1 to 5, skip number 3, then show the teacher. What tool helps Noah hold all that?

choices.t: Write the steps as a quick list
Keep it all in his head and rush
choices.why: Rushing makes the brain notepad spill. Writing it down holds the steps for him.

choices.t: Do the first step and stop
choices.why: The first step is a great start, but there are more. A list shows them all.

items.explain: Writing directions down moves them from your brain notepad onto paper, so nothing gets lost.
items.hint: Which choice puts the steps somewhere Noah can see?

items.prompt: Priya reads a long paragraph. By the end, she forgets the beginning. What can help?

choices.t: Stop after each part and say what it was about
Read faster so it ends sooner
choices.why: Speed does not help memory. Small stops give her brain time to save each part.
The last sentence leaves out most of the ideas. Short retells keep them all.

items.explain: Reading in chunks and retelling each one in your own words helps it stick.
items.hint: Which choice breaks the reading into small parts?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to paint a picture.
items.explain: You need paints before you can paint. You wash the brush when you are done.
items.hint: What do you need before you can paint?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to eat a banana.
items.explain: The peel comes off first. You throw it away after you eat.
items.hint: What do you do before you take a bite?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to build a snowman.
steps: ⚪ Roll a big ball for the bottom
⛄ Put a smaller ball on top
items.explain: The big ball goes on the bottom. The nose goes on the head, so the head must be on first.
items.hint: What part holds up the rest?

items.prompt: Your card says: “First clean up, then play.” What do you do first?

choices.why: Play comes next, after clean up. It is coming!
Sleep is not on the card. Look at the first picture.

items.explain: A first-then card shows the order. Do the first job, then you get the fun part!
items.hint: Look at the first picture.

items.prompt: You cannot find your crayons again. Where is a good place to keep them?

choices.t: In the same bin every day

choices.why: Things on the floor get lost or stepped on. One home spot is easy to find.
Under the bed is hard to see. A bin is easier.

items.explain: Giving things a “home” means you always know where to look.
items.hint: Which spot is the same every day?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to do your homework.
steps: 📚 Get out the supplies you need
items.explain: You need to know what is due before you pick supplies. Finished work goes in the folder last.
items.hint: How do you know which supplies you need?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to write a research report.
items.explain: A question tells you which facts to find. You sort the facts before you write.
items.hint: What tells you which facts to look for?

items.prompt: Owen has three chores: make his bed, feed the dog, and take out the trash. The trash truck comes in 10 minutes. Which chore should he do first?

choices.why: His bed can wait. The truck will not!
Fun is great, but the trash has a time limit. Start with what cannot wait.

items.explain: When a job has a deadline coming soon, do it first. This is called prioritizing.
items.hint: Which chore has a clock on it?

items.prompt: Lina keeps losing papers in her backpack. Which system could help?

choices.t: One folder: “To Do” on one side, “Done” on the other

choices.why: Papers get lost that way. A system gives each paper a home.

choices.t: Carry the papers in her hands all day
choices.why: Hands get tired and busy. A folder holds them for her.

items.explain: A simple folder system tells every paper where it belongs, so it is easy to find.
items.hint: Which choice gives papers a home?

items.prompt: Diego got a model rocket kit. What is a smart first step?

choices.t: Read all the directions and gather the parts

choices.why: Starting fast is exciting! Reading first helps avoid glue in the wrong spot.
Directions are a map. Keeping them helps him know each step.

items.explain: Planners look at the whole job and gather what they need before they start.
items.hint: Which choice looks at the whole plan first?

items.prompt: Put the steps of a school morning in order.
items.explain: You wake up first. You get dressed before you leave for school.
items.hint: What happens when your eyes open?

items.prompt: Put the seasons in order, starting with winter.
items.explain: After cold winter comes spring. Summer is next, then fall.
items.hint: When do flowers start to grow?

items.prompt: Which takes a shorter time?

choices.why: A beach day takes hours. A clap takes one second!

items.explain: A clap takes about one second. A beach day takes many hours.
items.hint: Which one is over in a snap?

items.prompt: The sand timer is almost empty. What does that mean?

choices.why: When time starts, the top is full. Almost empty means almost done.
The sand is falling like it should. It shows time moving.

items.explain: A sand timer lets you see time go. When the sand is almost gone, it is time to finish up.
items.hint: Is the top full or almost empty?

items.prompt: A grown-up says, “5 more minutes at the park.” What can you do?

choices.t: Pick one last short thing to do

choices.why: A long game will not fit in 5 minutes. Pick something short.
The warning helps you get ready. Listening makes leaving easier.

items.explain: A warning gives your brain time to get ready for a change. One last short fun thing is a great plan!
items.hint: Which choice fits in 5 minutes?

items.prompt: Put the school day in order by the clock.
items.explain: Morning times come before afternoon times. 8:00 in the morning is first, and 3:00 in the afternoon is last.
items.hint: Which time is in the morning?

items.prompt: Put these amounts of time in order, from shortest to longest.
items.explain: 60 seconds make a minute, 60 minutes make an hour, 24 hours make a day, and 7 days make a week.
items.hint: Which one is as quick as a blink?

items.prompt: Grace wants her morning to go more smoothly. Which tool helps her see time?

choices.t: A picture schedule with a timer for each step
Guess how long each step takes
choices.why: Guesses can be way off. A timer shows the real time.
Rushing can cause mix-ups, like two different socks! A schedule keeps her steady.

items.explain: A picture schedule shows what comes next, and a timer shows how much time is left.
items.hint: Which choice uses tools she can look at?

items.prompt: Marcus has a 30-minute reading goal. He reads 10 minutes, then takes a 5-minute break. How many more minutes does he need to read?

choices.why: Break time does not count as reading time. 30 − 10 = 20.
He read for 10 minutes, not 5. 30 − 10 = 20.

items.explain: He read 10 of his 30 minutes, so 20 are left. Short breaks between chunks help brains stay fresh!
items.hint: Only reading minutes count toward the goal.

items.prompt: Rosa often feels surprised when it is time to leave for soccer. What could help?

choices.t: Set an alarm to ring 10 minutes before leaving

choices.why: Others might forget too. An alarm is a helper she controls.
Remembering on time is hard for many brains. An alarm does the remembering.

items.explain: A warning alarm makes time visible, so leaving is not a surprise.
items.hint: Which choice does the remembering for her?

items.prompt: You want the blue cup, but it is dirty. What can you say?

choices.why: You might get thirsty. Another cup still holds water.

choices.t: “It has to be blue or nothing!”
choices.why: Blue is your favorite, and that is OK. Another cup can work today.

items.explain: Having a favorite is great. Saying “that is OK too” is flexible thinking.
items.hint: Which choice finds a Plan B cup?

items.prompt: Your block tower keeps falling down. What is a good Plan B?

choices.t: Build it the same way again and again
choices.why: The same way may fall the same way. Try something new!
That would make your friend sad. Try a new way to build yours.

items.explain: When one way does not work, try a new way. A wide bottom makes a strong tower.
items.hint: Which choice tries something different?

items.prompt: It is raining. Recess will be inside today. What can you do?

choices.t: Pick an inside game you like
Stand by the door and wait
choices.why: The rain may last a while. An inside game is fun now.
Recess is different today, not gone. Different is OK.

items.explain: Inside recess is a Plan B. Saying “different is OK” helps.
items.hint: Which choice is a new fun plan?

items.prompt: Oops! Your drawing has a smudge. What can you do?

choices.t: Turn the smudge into something new, like a cloud

choices.why: Your drawing has lots of good parts. A smudge can become something new.
One smudge does not change that. Artists fix smudges all the time.

items.explain: A mistake can turn into a new idea. That is flexible thinking!
items.hint: Which choice keeps your drawing?

items.prompt: Your class walks a new way to lunch today. You feel worried. What can you tell yourself?

choices.t: “New way, same lunch. I can do this.”
“I will only go the old way.”
choices.why: The class goes together. The new way still gets you to lunch.
Worry is OK. It is only a new hallway, and lunch is at the end!

items.explain: Kind self-talk helps with changes. Say what is new and what stays the same.
items.hint: Which words are calm and kind?

items.prompt: The bus is late, so morning meeting is skipped today. Aiden likes his schedule to stay the same. What helps most?

choices.t: Ask the teacher what the new schedule is
Insist on having morning meeting anyway
choices.why: Liking routines is real and OK. Knowing the new plan helps more than holding on to the old one.
Keeping worry inside can make it grow. Asking gives him a clear picture.

items.explain: When a schedule changes, knowing the new plan helps a brain feel calm. Asking is a great tool.
items.hint: Which choice gets Aiden clear information?

items.prompt: There are 4 bags with 5 apples in each. Mateo cannot remember 4 × 5. What is another strategy?

choices.why: Forgetting a fact is normal. Another strategy can still get there.
That makes 9. There are 4 groups of 5, so skip counting works better.

items.explain: 5, 10, 15, 20. Four groups of 5 make 20. When one way is stuck, try another!
items.hint: Count the apples bag by bag.

items.prompt: Hana is great at drawing, but writing is hard for her. Her teacher says students can show frog facts any way they like. What choice uses her strengths?

choices.t: Draw labeled pictures of a frog’s life cycle
Skip the project because writing is hard
choices.why: The teacher said any way works. Her drawing skills are a great fit!

choices.t: Copy a paragraph from a book
choices.why: Copying does not show her own learning. Her drawings can.

items.explain: There is more than one way to show what you know. Using your strengths is smart and flexible.
items.hint: What is Hana great at?

items.prompt: Eli thinks, “If I don’t get 100%, I failed.” He got 18 out of 20. Which thought is more flexible?

choices.t: “I got most right, and I can learn from 2.”
“I failed because it is not perfect.”
choices.why: 18 out of 20 is a lot right! Perfect is not the only kind of good.
Tests can help you learn. This thought skips the chance to grow.

items.explain: Flexible thinking sees more than all or nothing. Most right, plus something to learn, is a win.
items.hint: Which thought is kind and still helps Eli grow?

items.prompt: Jada keeps getting stuck on a hard video game level. What is a flexible move?

choices.t: Try a different path or ask how others beat it
Do the exact same thing 50 more times
choices.why: Practice helps, but if nothing changes, the result may not change. Switch it up!

choices.t: Decide she is bad at games
choices.why: One hard level does not decide that. A new strategy might be the key.

items.explain: Stuck is a signal to try a new strategy. Flexible thinkers switch it up.
items.hint: Which choice tries something new?

items.prompt: The paper says, “Draw 5 stars.” You drew these. What do you do?

choices.why: Count again: 4 is not 5 yet. One more!
Your 4 stars are good! Just add 1 more.

items.explain: Counting to check shows you need one more. 4 and 1 more makes 5.
items.hint: Count the stars. Is it 5?

items.prompt: Look at this sentence. What needs fixing?

choices.why: I is always a capital letter. Keep it!
A sentence needs a period at the end. Keep it!

items.explain: The letters in dgo got mixed up. Reading slowly, word by word, helps you catch it.
items.hint: Read each word slowly. Which word looks funny?

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to check your work.
items.explain: You finish first, then look it over. You hand it in last, after checking.
items.hint: What do you need before you can check?

items.prompt: You cleaned your room. How can you check it is really done?

choices.t: Look at your clean-up picture list

choices.why: A quick look with your list catches things you missed.
Checking needs open eyes! Look at your list.

items.explain: A picture list shows each job. Look at it to check nothing is left.
items.hint: Which choice uses a list?

items.prompt: Lily thinks there are 6 bugs. How can she check?

choices.t: Touch each bug and count again

choices.why: Fast counting can skip one. Touching each bug helps.
A guess does not check. Touch and count.

items.explain: Touching each one as you count keeps you from skipping. There are 5 bugs!
items.hint: Touch each bug as you say a number.

items.prompt: Put the steps in order to proofread your writing.
items.explain: You must read to find mistakes, and find them before you fix them. A last read makes sure the fixes worked.
items.hint: What must you do before you can mark a mistake?

items.prompt: Ruby wrote 6 × 4 = 28. Which check helps her?

choices.why: That makes 10. Adding does not check multiplying. Skip counting does.

choices.t: Trust it because she was fast
choices.why: Being fast is a strength, and a quick check still helps.

items.explain: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24. So 6 × 4 = 24, not 28. Skip counting caught the slip!
items.hint: 6 × 4 means 6 groups of 4.

items.prompt: The directions said, “Circle the nouns.” Oscar underlined the verbs. What check would have helped?

choices.why: Speed was not the problem. Rereading the directions catches mix-ups.
Guessing is how the mix-up happened. Directions tell you the job.

items.explain: Reading directions twice, and underlining key words like “circle” and “nouns,” helps you do what is asked.
items.hint: Where did Oscar find out what to do?

items.prompt: Tia added 198 + 203 and got 1,401. What quick check shows the answer is off?

choices.t: Count how many digits there are
choices.why: Counting digits does not tell if the sum is right. Rounding gives a close guess.

choices.t: Write the answer in a new color
choices.why: The color does not change the math. Rounding shows 1,401 is too big.

items.explain: 198 + 203 is about 400, so 1,401 is way too big. The real answer is 401.
items.hint: What are 198 and 203 each close to?

items.prompt: Before turning in a test, Sofia uses a checklist. Which question belongs on it?

choices.why: Finishing first is not the goal. Answering every question is.
Fun pencils are great, but that does not check the work.

items.explain: A good checklist asks about the work: every question answered, name on top, answers that make sense.
items.hint: Which question is about the test itself?
